text:
sam: Heads-up -- I put together a short proposal to change admission control when GPUs are saturated. Instead of hard rejects, experiment with a lightweight token-pacing/degrade layer that slows long-running requests and preserves short ones. Thoughts?

priya: Curious about user-visible effects. Will this just increase tail latency or will calls get 429s?

sam: The idea is to avoid 100% immediate 429s. We’d introduce a per-tenant pacing window that caps token emission rate; if a request exceeds a short queue timeout it still gets a 429. So some requests get slower, not instantly rejected.

luca: Does pacing require per-request KV cache pinning? If we slow generation we might hold KV cache longer and hurt throughput.

meng: Good call. We can implement pacing as a token-budget limiter that pauses generation callbacks, but we should include a fast-path cutoff to release KV cache after X ms to avoid pinning memory.

mike: From SLOs perspective customers care more about median/95 than rare long tails. But enterprise SLAs might prefer immediate rejects to keep latency predictable. Need to surface per-customer policy.

priya: Also cost: if requests sit longer they keep GPU occupied, net throughput could drop and cost per token could increase. Have we modeled CPU/GPU inefficiency from paused contexts?

sam: We ran a small sim last week. Basic numbers: pacing at 0.8x token rate reduced 429s by ~60% and increased average GPU occupancy by ~7%. Net tokens/sec dropped ~5% but customer-visible failures dropped. I can paste the sim output.

sam: ```
sim summary:
 - baseline (reject): 200k tokens/s, 14% of requests 429 under spike
 - pacing 0.8x: 190k tokens/s, 5% 429, avg latency +120ms on affected requests
 - pacing + fast-drop: 195k tokens/s, 2% 429, KV pin time capped at 150ms
```

luca: That fast-drop parameter matters. If KV pinned > 200ms we blow memory headroom. We should set conservative default and allow per-pool overrides.

meng: We also need observability hooks: tokens_delayed, kv_pinned_ms, pacing_active boolean, per-tenant backlog. Add a rollout flag so we can flip pacing on for specific fleet pools.

mike: What about API semantics? If a request is slowed, the client may think the network is flaky and retry. We need clear headers and a Retry-After or info in the streaming preamble. Otherwise retries could amplify load.

sam: Absolutely. Plan: when pacing engages we send a small control frame at stream start: `{"x-rdwd-admit": "pacing", "rate": "0.8x"}` and for queued requests we add `Retry-After` header. Also docs update.

priya: Can we combine with short-queue (10ms) + pacing? So we queue briefly for bursts, then pace the overflow. That keeps tail latency low for short spikes.

meng: Yes, staged approach: 1) tiny in-memory queue (burst absorb), 2) pacing, 3) reject after T_max. We must tune T_max per model-size and pool.

luca: Implementation details: admission controller should run before model dispatch to avoid unnecessary model load. Also add fairness token buckets so one tenant doesn't hog pacing slack.

sam: Agreed on fairness. We'll prototype on a small pool in us-west-2, low-risk customers only. Rollout steps in PR: config flags, telemetry, docs, canary for 48h, then expand.

mike: Add test cases in the load harness for mixed short/long requests and for KV pressure scenarios. Also smoke tests ensuring headers are emitted.

deploy-bot: Deploy scheduled: branch=admit/pacing-experiment, target=canary/us-west-2, eta=tomorrow 10:00 PDT.

priya: +1 but block until we have Retry-After header and run two quick perf runs with KV pinning toggled.

sam: Will do. I'll open the PR and include sim data and runbook for reverting to hard-reject if we see SLA regressions. Thanks all :+1:

mike: If possible also expose a per-tenant toggle in console so sales/success can opt-out high-SLA customers during the experiment.

sam: Noted. I’ll add a flag and coordinate with PMs.

meng: I'll add the telemetry and alert thresholds (pacing ratio > 50% for 5m, kv_pin_ms p90 > 120ms).

luca: I'll review the PR for KV lifecycle handling.

sam: Great — PR link when ready.
